CHAIR ( Senator Cox ): I declare open this hearing of the Committee Affairs Legislation committee into the 2025-26 supplementary budget estimates. I begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we meet today and I pay my respects to their elders, past and present. I extend that respect to all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people here today. The committee has fixed Friday 28 November 2025 as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice. The committee would appreciate if senators could please provide any written questions on notice to the secretariat by Thursday 16 October 2025. The committee's proceedings today will begin with the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing outcome 4, Disability and carers. The committee will be conducting today's hearing in person and via videoconference.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session. This includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that in giving evidence to the committee they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee and such action shall be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance for questions at Senate estimate hearings. Any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funding in estimates are relevant questions for the purposes of Senate estimates hearings. I remind all officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved also that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked of the officer to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. Witnesses are reminded of the Senate's orders specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised. I incorporate the public interest immunity statement into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

CHAIR: I now welcome Senator the Hon. Jenny McAllister, Minister for the National Disability Insurance Scheme, representing the Minister for Health, Disability and Ageing. Minister, do you wish to make an opening statement?

Senator McAllister: I do. Thank you. I thank the committee for the opportunity to say a few words. It's my first opportunity to appear before this committee. I want to acknowledge the enormous privilege and the honour I feel at being asked to be a steward for the NDIS. It is not a responsibility that I take lightly. The NDIS is a world-leading scheme, and our government is committed to the NDIS as a key pillar of the Australian social safety net. We're focused on a sustainable scheme that can continue to provide life-changing supports for people with significant and permanent disability. It's around 150 days since I was sworn in, and, in that time, many disability leaders have been incredibly generous in giving their time and their hard-won expertise to help me learn about this portfolio. This has helped me to understand where to focus and built the foundations for positive working relationships with the disability community. I'd like to express my gratitude to those who have engaged with me so thoughtfully and so constructively. I want in particular to thank the members of the NDIS Reform Advisory Committee, co-chaired by El Gibbs and Dougie Herd, for providing their insight and their advice on the NDIS reforms.

Our government's purpose is to build the very best scheme that we can focused on the needs of people with disability. During the last term, the government received wide-ranging advice from the independent review into the NDIS, the disability royal commission, the Provider and Worker Registration Taskforce and others. In particular, the NDIS review described how it is in the interests of everyone, including people with disability, service providers and governments, to secure the future sustainability of the NDIS. Subsequently, we've been progressing reforms that enhance the sustainability and the integrity of the scheme.

Much of the advice that we received points to the need for a unified system of disability supports so that the NDIS is not the only port in the storm. In August, Minister Butler spoke about this government's intention to establish Thriving Kids to provide foundational supports for children under nine with low to moderate support needs in line with the NDIS review findings. The goal is to establish another layer of support, a second tier, to make sure we're offering families a straightforward, timely and lower cost way to access support. We know that we can do better for many of these children and their families, and we will be working with states and territories to develop this national system of supports. In this, we seek the guidance and collaboration with the disability community. Minister Butler has referred an inquiry into the Thriving Kids initiative to the House Standing Committee on Health, Aged Care and Disability, and there is a public hearing happening concurrently with today's estimates hearings. Minister Butler is co-chairing the Thriving Kids Advisory Group along with Professor Frank Oberklaid AM, and I welcome his invitation to the NDIS Reform Advisory Committee to engage with the program design work.

One of my priorities for this portfolio is improving the participant experience in terms of the way that participants engage with the NDIA. As the NDIS review identified, the current approach to planning is inconsistent, confusing and often cost intensive for participants and their families. The NDIS review recommended a fairer approach to planning that is easier to navigate. Recently, we announced that we are partnering with the University of Melbourne and the Centre for Disability Studies to develop a new approach to framework planning using the Instrument for the Classification and Assessment of Support Needs, or ICAN. This new approach will put a structured conversation at the heart of the planning process. Accredited assessors will meet with participants and their families and supporters as necessary to have a strengths based conversation to understand their individual disability support needs. The ICAN will be used alongside questionnaires on each participant's personal and environmental circumstances. Importantly, this process will be collaborative. It will provide opportunities for the assessor to play back what they have heard and for the participants, their families and supporters to ensure the information is accurate. This simpler, more transparent approach will give participants greater clarity about how their needs are being assessed.

I acknowledge there is a lot more to be done. I want to thank disability representative organisations for their considered advocacy in making it clear we need to be careful and not rush rollout of the new planning framework. This is important. We have listened to them and moved the start of the rollout to the middle of next year so that there is time to get it right.

As minister, I must make it clear that I am committed to a scheme that operates safely and with integrity. Those who defraud the NDIS are exploiting hundreds of thousands of Australians who rely on the life-changing support the NDIS delivers. I have issued an updated Statement of Expectations for the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission. This statement outlines the government's priorities to uplift quality, ensure safety and take a hard line on fraud in the NDIS as the commission continues to mature as a regulator. Every dollar taken by fraud is a dollar taken by someone who needs it. Where we see fraud, we often see a range of other harms to participants—from low quality services to abuse, neglect or exploitation. After a decade of neglect, Labor has taken fraud seriously. We have invested over $500 million in tackling fraud and noncompliance and more than $470 million to ensure the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission has the resources it needs to ensure Australians with disability get the support that they deserve. I thank the senators and members from across the parliament who have worked collegiately with me since my appointment. I know that the disability community wants to see elected officials working together to support them. I look forward to continuing to work across the parliament to ensure we are reaching the best possible outcomes for NDIS participants and for the broader disability community.

CHAIR: I also welcome the Secretary of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Mr Blair Comley PSM. Mr Comley, do you wish to make an opening statement today?

CHAIR: I now call officers of the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing in relation to outcome 4, Disability and carers, and invite questions. Can the minister please table her opening statement?

Senator McAllister: I can.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: Minister, I thank you and your office for your briefing in relation to the Duckett review, which was really useful. Firstly, I refer to Thriving Kids. On 20 August the government announced the Thriving Kids initiative, presenting it to the community as a pathway, an opportunity, to restore broad-based support for infants, children and parents so that kids can thrive outside the NDIS. On 21 August, the minister was asked a question that was on the minds of a lot of community members after that announcement, which was: how will kids with autism or developmental delay be placed into different categories—mild, moderate et cetera? In answer to that question the minister stated that will ultimately be a clinical determination. Is the minister able to provide a bit more information or insight into how these categories will be defined for children under nine?

Senator McAllister: I acknowledge your willingness to engage with me over recent months since I came into the role. You're correct; the government is establishing Thriving Kids, because we do recognise that for children with low to moderate support needs we think there are better alternatives. We heard that advice through the review that was provided to us by Professor Bonyhady and Lisa Paul. I think in the public statements that you've referenced Minister Butler has made it clear that there are design questions to work through. This is a program that was first canvassed by the review in its discussion of foundational supports. In 2023 National Cabinet agreed to progress a system of foundational supports for children, and we are keen to see this come about. I think that the department can speak to you a little more about the way we are thinking about some of these design questions. I emphasise that we are at the beginning of that process. We've asked Professor Oberklaid to co-chair the working group, as I alluded to in my opening statement. We're also very interested in the feedback that we'll hear through the committee work that Dr Freelander is leading.

Mr Mansfield : As the minister indicated, the advisory group that's being co-chaired by Professor Oberklaid is very much looking at the elements of the design as part of that. That goes to things like: How do you try to drive earlier identification of children who may have developmental concerns and delay or disability? Once identified, how do you, as quickly as possible, get them into the supports that they and their families need? In terms of the question around the process by which people will be identified as having low or moderate support needs, that process is still part of that design work. It's also part of discussions with states and territories in terms of the negotiations that are underway. We are very much in the middle of engaging with states and territories around some of the assumptions that go to the questions that you've asked, as well as working through the design elements which include which children will go into Thriving Kids, how they'll be supported through that and indeed through mainstream systems, as well as those children who will continue to be supported through the NDIS.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: At this moment, you are not able to share with us who will be placed into the mild or moderate category; is that correct?

Mr Mansfield : That's still part of the design process.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: What clinicians will be at the head of that process? Are you able to shed any light on that?

Mr Mansfield : That's also part of the design process. It is very much looking at how people are identified and then how they will move through the system. There's obviously a strong focus on family capacity building as well. As you would appreciate, people can be identified in many different settings. They may be identified by an early childhood educator who indicates there may be an issue. They may be identified through the child maternal health system, which may indicate that there is a need for support. They may be identified through a GP or a nurse practitioner. We very much want to leverage as much as we can those existing systems and processes for identifying and getting people into support. There is a focus on enabling that to occur as rapidly as possible.

Senator STEELE-JOHN: So we have the role of the clinician and the categories questions are still in the design phase. The government stated that the Inklings program will be for kids up to three years old; is that correct?

Mr Mansfield : The minister identified that as one initiative that exists today which is being trialled in WA, as you would know, as well as in South Australia, and use that as an example of the kinds of supports that may be beneficial for children at the younger age. Senator ANTIC: Thanks, Chair. This is a handful of questions. I'm interested in the justification for the use of funds intended to support women who've been through the grief of a stillborn baby. Through the parenting payment, those funds have been used for an abortion after 20 weeks and up to birth. What is the rationale for that payment being made in those circumstances?

Under the family assistance act, a stillborn child needs to weigh at least 400 grams at delivery or be a child whose period of gestation was at least 20 weeks and who has not breathed since delivery and whose heart has not beaten since delivery. A qualified medical professional is required to provide written evidence that the stillborn child was delivered.

Senator ANTIC: All of which is as it is. But it is the case, is it not, that if a woman—presumably, not a 'person'—has an abortion after 20 weeks and up to birth, she is eligible for that payment in those circumstances?

Mr Flavel : I think what you would be describing are circumstances in which the medical professional is certifying or suggesting that an abortion is a stillborn.

Senator ANTIC: Is that the intent of the payment fund? Was that the original intent of it?

Mr Flavel : The intent, as per the name, is to make a payment in respect of the incredibly tragic circumstances in which somebody might find themselves with a stillborn baby.

Senator ANTIC: Does the department collect data from the application form as to whether the applicant had a tragic natural stillbirth or an abortion?

Mr Flavel : Services Australia collects this information in the forms for the purposes of processing the payment. I'm happy to check, on notice, but, as I said, it's the medical professional who is certifying that it's a stillborn baby, for the purposes of the payment.

Mr Flavel : What I will say is that we're not aware of circumstances in which the payment is being claimed for abortion. I'm happy to check with Services Australia whether they have any documentary evidence. Certainly, from what I've seen, the certification process by the medical professional and the way in which the process itself works does not allow for circumstances in which somebody has an abortion and then claims the stillborn baby payment.

Senator ANTIC: Is paid parental leave accessible in those circumstances, if someone were to have an abortion after 20 weeks and up to birth? Are you entitled to both payments in those circumstances?

Mr Flavel : I'm not going to characterise it in that way. You keep referring to abortion. There are a set of arrangements around a stillborn baby and what occurs in the tragic circumstances of a stillborn birth. Ms Hunter : That is correct.

Senator ASKEW: Is there a reason for that? Perhaps the minister might like to answer that one.

Senator McAllister: The government is aware of the significance of closing the gap. We're also conscious of the potential of this position. There have been a number of discussions with First Nations stakeholders about the relevant powers and the future powers for the national commissioner, and those discussions will inform the approach to legislation.

Senator ASKEW: Is there a timeframe around when they'll be tabled?

Senator McAllister: We're working on it, and we'll take the time to get that right.

Senator ASKEW: Is it a question we ask again in December, or do we wait till next year? Is it imminent or not? That's probably my main question.

Senator ASKEW: What powers will the commission have, then? For example, can it compel the provision of state data, which is obviously a big issue with the closing of the gaps, or undertake audits of service providers who have important work to do?

Senator McAllister: As I understand it, the previous Indigenous affairs opposition spokesperson said in the lead-up to the election that they would abolish the position if they won. I'm not clear what the position of the coalition is at the moment.

Senator ASKEW: I'm just trying to understand where it's at. It's not very clear where it's at, really, at this point. You've made a commitment. You've put a commissioner in place. Ms Hunter : After my five weeks, what the commission has currently started doing has been making a framework to start to work with getting the voices of children to be put into place to advise government of their wishes. Senator ASKEW: The consultations with states—how's that being undertaken?

Ms Hope : I might be able to help there. Establishing the national commissioner as an executive agency was the first step to legislating the national commissioner. Ms Hunter's predecessor, who was acting in the role for that period of time, has been working with those commissioners, advocates and guardians around looking at what issues need to be addressed as part of systemic gaps across the Safe and Supported framework and how the Commonwealth and the states can work together on these issues around both promoting and protecting the rights of First Nations children and young people; providing advice to government to inform the implementation of those key policy frameworks; promoting cross-coordination between the Commonwealth, states, territories and non-government organisations in the First Nations sector, which is a really important role. I think Ms Hrast also talked about an Office for Youth Forum that was held in, I think, September last year—I can't quite recall but around that time. Senator ASKEW: You mentioned that two states hadn't been consulted with yet. Which states are those?

Ms Hunter : That would be Tasmania and Western Australia.

Ms Hrast : That's the actual children's commissioners. It's a direct conversation with those children's commissioners.

Ms Hunter : We're working on it at the moment.
